title: The emperor under the blankets
told: from the notebook of Marcus Aurelius

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? how many times did you hit snooze this week?
options: same. you’re about to meet a fellow snoozer.
lucky. you’ll still know this argument.

steps.line: Remember Marcus Aurelius, the emperor with the notebook? One cold morning, he lay under his blankets, and did not want to get up.
So he argued with himself, in writing. When you rise unwillingly, he told himself, remember: “I am rising to the work of a human being.”
“Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?” Then he answered himself: but this is more pleasant.

steps.q: Why would the most powerful man in the world argue with his own blankets?
o: Even emperors fight small battles daily
He was drafting a speech for his troops
His doctors had told him to stay in bed
steps.why: Power doesn’t make the warm bed any less warm. And the notebook was private, written to himself, not to an audience.

steps.q: To win the argument, where does Marcus look?
o: At the little creatures, busy at their work
At the maps of his empire
steps.why: Not at his power. At ants and bees.

steps.line: He looked at the little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, all busy doing their part to keep the world in order.
And you, a human being, he asked himself, won’t do a human’s work?
For a Stoic, a human’s work was simple to say: be kind, be fair, be useful to the people around you.

steps.q: Marcus never called his notebook Meditations. What do the old manuscripts title it?
steps.why: In Greek, Ta eis heauton: things to himself. He wrote in Greek, much of it in army camps on the Danube, and most likely never meant anyone else to read it.

steps.line: Today: the alarm, the warm covers, the bargaining. Get up, not to be impressive, but because there’s a human’s work waiting.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Marcus pushes back on himself: “But I need rest, too.” What does he answer?
o: “Then rest, but only once the work is done.”
“Yes, but nature sets a limit on it.”
“Rest is fine, if it helps you work better.”
steps.why: “But nature has set limits to that, as to eating and drinking.” He wasn’t against rest. He just noticed he’d gone past enough.

say: here’s what i love. this isn’t a hero who never struggled. it’s a tired man winning a tiny argument, and writing it down so he’d remember.
marcus wrote that people are made to work together, like hands, like feet, like the upper and lower teeth. for him, the alarm wasn’t a punishment. it was a call back to that shared work.

steps.q: Marcus never says “get up because the empire needs you.” Why does that matter for someone who isn’t an emperor?
o: It only works if your job is big
He secretly didn’t care about the empire
Anyone has a human’s work to do
steps.why: His reason fits a nurse, a student, a parent. Anyone who is a human being.

today.say: tomorrow morning, at the first alarm, ask marcus’s question: what’s the human’s work waiting for me today? name one: a person to be kind to, a job to do well. then feet on the floor.
options: once is how marcus did it too. one morning at a time.

tomorrow.line: an enslaved man’s master twists his leg. what he says next is still taught today.

sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 5.1 (George Long, 1862): “In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present: I am rising to the work of a human being”; “Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm? But this is more pleasant”; the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees working together to put in order their several parts of the universe.
Meditations 2.1 (Long): “we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth.”
